# 7 Alternatives to Roblox for Kids (2026 Parent Guide)

9/16/2026

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Focqt1g5c%2Fproduction%2Fea42b07563f55b87312e53ae45262521a52cd625-1672x941.png&w=3840&q=75)

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Focqt1g5c%2Fproduction%2Fea42b07563f55b87312e53ae45262521a52cd625-1672x941.png%3Fw%3D1600%26fit%3Dmax%26auto%3Dformat&w=3840&q=75)

Good alternatives to Roblox for kids include TruPlay (for Christian families), Toca Boca World, PBS KIDS Games, Scratch and ScratchJr, LEGO Worlds, Minecraft and Animal Jam. The right pick depends on what your child loves about Roblox, whether that's building, role-play, making games or playing with friends, and how much contact with other players you're comfortable with.

A quick note: we make TruPlay. For every other pick, we checked chat and purchases on the company's own site, its store listing or its ESRB rating in September 2026, so take a fresh look before you download. For Roblox's own settings, see our [Complete Parents' Guide to Roblox](https://www.truplaygames.com/blog/complete-parents-guide-to-roblox).

## 7 Roblox alternatives, roughly in order from closed play to social play

### 1. TruPlay: for Christian families

* **Who it suits:** Families who want faith woven into play. The app has 35+ games, comics and videos. Games include [King David's Battles](https://www.truplaygames.com/games/king-davids-battles) (an action RPG drawn from 1 Samuel 16 and 17) and [Stained Glass](https://www.truplaygames.com/games/stained-glass) (a match-3 game retelling stories from Genesis and Exodus), and the comics and videos feature stories from The Action Bible and Book of God.
* **Ages:** Built for kids 4 to 12, and each game on the [games page](https://www.truplaygames.com/games) has its own label, from 3+ to 8+.
* **Chat:** None. There are no chatrooms, and kids can't message other players.
* **Ads and purchases:** [No ads](https://www.truplaygames.com/blog/is-truplay-ad-free) and nothing to buy inside the games. The subscription is [$12.99 a month or $69.99 a year](https://www.truplaygames.com/blog/truplay-pricing), new accounts get a 7-day free trial, and one subscription covers up to 10 profiles. You play in the app on iPhone, iPad and Android devices.

### 2. Toca Boca World: for young role-players

* **Who it suits:** Kids who love Roblox role-play. They design characters, decorate homes and make up stories across [90+ locations](https://www.tocaboca.com/toca-boca-world).
* **Ages:** Rated 4+ on the App Store.
* **Chat:** None. [Toca Boca describes it](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/toca-boca-world-game-play/id1208138685) as a single-player game with no chat and no strangers.
* **Ads and purchases:** Free to download, with no third-party ads. Optional in-app packs cost extra (a recent style pack was $2.99), and some events feature brands such as adidas.

### 3. PBS KIDS Games: for preschool and early grades

* **Who it suits:** Younger siblings who want short learning games with characters like Daniel Tiger.
* **Ages:** [280+ free curriculum-based games](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/pbs-kids-games/id1050773989) for ages 2 to 8, rated 4+ on the App Store.
* **Chat:** [PBS KIDS says](https://pbskids.org/privacy) anything kids post through its interactive features is canned or moderated.
* **Ads and purchases:** Free, with no in-app purchases listed on the App Store. PBS won't use children's personal information for marketing or online advertising, though its services can carry underwriting (sponsor) messages.

### 4. Scratch and ScratchJr: for kids who want to make games

* **Who it suits:** Kids who like the creating side of Roblox. They snap code blocks together to make games, stories and animations.
* **Ages:** Scratch is designed for ages 8 to 16. ScratchJr is a simpler version for ages 5 to 7.
* **Chat:** Scratch has an online community where kids share projects and comment. [The Scratch Team manages activity](https://scratch.mit.edu/parents/) and responds to reports, with help from a profanity filter. ScratchJr saves projects on the device.
* **Cost:** Both are free, and Scratch is run by a nonprofit.

### 5. LEGO Worlds: for LEGO fans who love to build

* **Who it suits:** Kids who want a digital LEGO sandbox for building worlds brick by brick.
* **Ages:** [ESRB Everyone 10+](https://www.esrb.org/ratings/34783/lego-worlds/) for cartoon violence.
* **Chat and online play:** Single-player, split-screen and online multiplayer. The ESRB doesn't rate online interactions, so set family settings on Steam or your console first.
* **Cost:** A paid game for PC and consoles, first released in 2017.

### 6. Minecraft: for kids who love to build and explore

* **Who it suits:** Roblox fans who love building. Creative mode focuses on building, and our [Complete Parents' Guide to Minecraft](https://www.truplaygames.com/blog/complete-parents-guide-to-minecraft) goes deeper.
* **Ages:** ESRB Everyone 10+ and [a recommended PEGI 7](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/parents--guide-minecraft). Combat is cartoony, with no blood.
* **Chat and online play:** Multiplayer is off by default on child accounts (under 16 in the US). [In Xbox family settings](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/parental-controls), parents choose who can reach their child by voice, text or invites: Everyone, Friends or Block.
* **Cost and purchases:** A paid game. Bedrock Edition has a Marketplace of maps, skins and mini-games bought with Minecoins, and Realms (a personal server for playing with friends) is a separate subscription.

### 7. Animal Jam: for kids who want to play with friends

* **Who it suits:** Animal-loving kids who miss playing with friends. Players dress up their animals, design dens and learn about real animals and their habitats.
* **Ages:** Rated 9+ on the App Store.
* **Chat:** Yes. [WildWorks says](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/animal-jam/id1003820457) chat is filtered and monitored, with live moderation and block and report tools. Parents control access to social features in Parent Tools.
* **Cost and purchases:** Free to play with a parent's permission, plus optional in-app purchases and a recurring membership.

## How to choose a Roblox alternative

1. Start with what your child loves about Roblox. Building points to Minecraft or LEGO Worlds, role-play to Toca Boca World or Animal Jam, making games to Scratch, short learning games to PBS KIDS Games, and faith-filled adventure to TruPlay.
2. Decide how much contact with other players feels right. If the answer is none, start with TruPlay, Toca Boca World or ScratchJr, or keep multiplayer switched off on a Minecraft child account.
3. Check how money gets spent. Subscriptions, paid games, in-app packs and memberships all work differently, so turn on purchase approvals on your child's device.
4. Read the rating, then play it yourself for an evening before you hand it over.
5. Look at the story, not only the settings. Ask what the game celebrates and what it teaches about kindness, courage and truth.

## FAQ

### What is a good Roblox alternative for a 6-year-old?

Look for games without open chat. Toca Boca World (rated 4+), ScratchJr (made for ages 5 to 7) and PBS KIDS Games (ages 2 to 8) all fit. On TruPlay, good places to start at this age are [Chirp Song: Wings of Praise](https://www.truplaygames.com/games/chirp-song-wings-of-praise), where kids free bird-like Chirps who sing the Psalms, and [Oliver and the Vindictive Vines](https://www.truplaygames.com/games/oliver-and-the-vindictive-vines).

### Is Minecraft safer than Roblox?

It can be. Multiplayer starts off on child accounts, and parents choose who can contact their child by voice, text or invites. Once multiplayer is on, public servers raise the same questions about strangers, so the settings matter more than the game.

### What about LEGO Fortnite?

LEGO Fortnite Odyssey is an island inside Fortnite, and [its page](https://www.fortnite.com/@epic/lego-fortnite-odyssey) lists "Users Interact" and "In-Game Purchases." [Epic's parental controls](https://safety.epicgames.com/en-US/parental-controls) let parents set voice and text chat permissions, require a PIN for real-money purchases made with Epic payments, and choose whether V-Bucks can be spent on random-reward items. Our [parents' guide to Fortnite](https://www.truplaygames.com/blog/parents-guide-to-fortnite) walks through the setup.

### Is there a Christian alternative to Roblox?

Yes. TruPlay is a Christian app for kids 4 to 12 with Bible-based games, comics and videos. Games like King David's Battles and Stained Glass retell Bible stories, and there are no ads, no chatrooms and nothing to buy inside the games. It's $12.99 a month or $69.99 a year, and new accounts can [try it free for 7 days](https://www.truplaygames.com/).

# 7 Safer Alternatives to Roblox That Still Let Kids Build and Create

**TL;DR:** If you're looking to diversify beyond [Roblox](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/roblox-game) (or step away entirely), here are the best platforms that still scratch that creative itch:

* **[Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game)** - The OG creative sandbox, ages 7+
* **[Core](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/core-game)** - Like Roblox but with better moderation, ages 10+
* **[Dreams](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/dreams-game)** - PlayStation's artistic creation platform, ages 12+
* **[LEGO Worlds](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/lego-worlds-game)** - Digital LEGO building, ages 7+
* **[Crayta](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/crayta-game)** - Collaborative game creation, ages 10+
* **[Tinkercad](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/tinkercad-app)** - 3D design for actual learning, ages 8+
* **[Scratch](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/scratch-app)** - MIT's coding platform, ages 8+

## Screenwise Parents

[See all](/videos)

Why Look Beyond Roblox?

Let's be clear: Roblox isn't inherently evil. It's genuinely impressive as a platform for user-generated content, and the entrepreneurial aspects are real. Some kids are learning actual game design principles and even making money.

**But.** The safety concerns are also real. The predator stories aren't just fear-mongering. The in-game purchases can spiral fast ([learn more about how Robux works![](/favicons/favicon-32x32.png)](https://chat.screenwiseapp.com/?prompt=how%20does%20robux%20spending%20work)). The content moderation is inconsistent at best. And honestly? A lot of the games are just... not that good. Low-effort cash grabs designed to extract Robux from kids who don't know better.

So whether you're looking to supplement Roblox with something else, or you're ready to make a clean break, here are platforms that offer similar creative freedom with better guardrails.

[Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game)

**Ages 7+ | PC, Console, Mobile**

Yeah, it's obvious. But Minecraft remains the gold standard for a reason. It's what Roblox wants to be when it grows up.

**What makes it better:** Single-player mode means your kid can create without any social pressure or stranger danger. When they do want multiplayer, you can set up private realms with known friends only. The modding community is massive but you control what gets installed. And the educational value is undeniable - redstone circuits teach actual logic, building teaches spatial reasoning, and the survival mode teaches resource management.

**The catch:** It's not a social platform in the same way. Your kid won't stumble onto 10,000 random games. But honestly? That's a feature, not a bug. Check out our [guide to Minecraft parental controls](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/minecraft-parental-controls) to set it up right.

**Cost:** $26.95 one-time purchase (realms subscription optional at $7.99/month)

[Core](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/core-game)

**Ages 10+ | PC**

If your kid specifically loves the "play random user-generated games" aspect of Roblox, Core is the closest alternative. It's built on Unreal Engine, so the graphics are significantly better, and the moderation is notably more robust.

**What makes it better:** The creator tools are more sophisticated, which means there's a higher barrier to entry - but also higher quality output. The community skews slightly older and more serious about game development. And the monetization is less predatory (though still exists).

**The catch:** It's PC only, and the system requirements are steeper than Roblox. Your kid needs a decent gaming computer. The smaller user base means fewer games to discover, but again, quality over quantity.

**Cost:** Free to play

[Dreams](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/dreams-game)

**Ages 12+ | PlayStation 4/5**

This is the artsy, sophisticated older sibling of creation platforms. Made by Media Molecule (the [LittleBigPlanet](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/littlebigplanet-game) folks), Dreams is less about churning out games and more about genuine creative expression.

**What makes it better:** The creation tools are wild - kids can make games, music, animations, interactive art. It's genuinely educational in terms of game design principles. The community is smaller and more curated. And because it's PlayStation exclusive, there's an extra layer of platform-level moderation.

**The catch:** The learning curve is STEEP. This isn't "drag and drop some blocks and make an obby." Your kid needs patience and genuine interest in creation, not just consumption. Best for tweens and teens who are serious about digital art or game design.

**Cost:** $29.99 one-time purchase

[LEGO Worlds](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/lego-worlds-game)

**Ages 7+ | PC, Console**

Imagine Minecraft but everything is LEGO. That's it. That's the pitch.

**What makes it better:** The LEGO brand means built-in safety. It's designed for kids. The building mechanics are intuitive if your kid has ever touched actual LEGO. There's a structured adventure mode alongside free build. And multiplayer is limited to split-screen or private sessions.

**The catch:** It's not as robust as Minecraft, and development has basically stopped (last major update was 2017). Think of it as a stepping stone - great for younger kids (7-10) who aren't ready for Minecraft's complexity but want that creative freedom.

**Cost:** $29.99 one-time purchase (often on sale)

[Crayta](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/crayta-game)

**Ages 10+ | PC, Stadia**

Another "make games and play games" platform, but with a focus on collaborative creation. Kids can build together in real-time, which is genuinely cool.

**What makes it better:** The real-time collaborative editing is unique - multiple kids can work on the same game simultaneously. The tutorials are excellent. And it's owned by Facebook Gaming, which means... okay, that's not necessarily better, but the moderation tools are decent.

**The catch:** Stadia is basically dead, so you're looking at PC only. The user base is small. And yes, it's Meta-adjacent, which gives some parents pause.

**Cost:** Free to play

[Tinkercad](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/tinkercad-app)

**Ages 8+ | Web Browser**

Okay, this isn't a game platform. But if what you value about Roblox is the *creation* aspect, Tinkercad is incredible. It's Autodesk's free 3D design platform, and it's shockingly kid-friendly.

**What makes it better:** Your kid is learning actual CAD software. The designs can be 3D printed (if you have access to a printer). There's a whole curriculum built in. And it's completely single-player - no social features, no strangers, no chat.

**The catch:** It's not a game. There's no "playing" what you create (though there are circuits and code blocks for basic interactions). This is for the kid who genuinely wants to *design*, not just play.

**Cost:** Free

[Scratch](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/scratch-app)

**Ages 8+ | Web Browser**

MIT's block-based coding platform. If your kid is interested in the game-making side of Roblox, Scratch teaches actual programming concepts in a visual, accessible way.

**What makes it better:** It's educational. Like, genuinely educational. Kids learn loops, conditionals, variables, and functions. The community is moderated by MIT. And there's a massive library of tutorials and projects to remix.

**The catch:** The games are simple. We're talking 2D, basic graphics, nothing flashy. But that's the point - your kid is learning the fundamentals. Many professional game developers started on Scratch.

**Cost:** Free

Age-Appropriate Guidance

**Ages 7-9:** Start with [Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game) in creative mode or [LEGO Worlds](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/lego-worlds-game). Keep it single-player or local multiplayer only. [Scratch](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/scratch-app) is great if they show interest in how games work.

**Ages 10-12:** [Core](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/core-game) and [Crayta](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/crayta-game) become viable options. [Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game) with friends-only realms. [Tinkercad](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/tinkercad-app) for the design-minded kid.

**Ages 13+:** [Dreams](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/dreams-game) if they're serious about creation. All of the above with more freedom. Consider whether they're ready for actual game engines like Unity or Unreal (with supervision).

What Parents Should Know

**None of these are perfect replacements.** Roblox's massive social network and endless content library is its primary draw. These alternatives trade that breadth for depth, safety, or educational value.

**Your kid will probably complain at first.** "But all my friends are on Roblox!" is a real concern. Consider a hybrid approach - maybe Roblox is allowed for 30 minutes of social time, but creative time happens in [Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game) or [Scratch](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/scratch-app).

**The "worse graphics" complaint is valid.** [Scratch](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/scratch-app) looks basic because it is basic. [LEGO Worlds](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/lego-worlds-game) is blocky because it's LEGO. Help your kid understand that limitations can breed creativity - some of the best games ever made had terrible graphics.

**Creation takes time.** Roblox lets kids instantly jump between hundreds of games. These platforms require patience and investment. That's actually good - it teaches delayed gratification and the satisfaction of building something yourself.

The Bottom Line

Roblox isn't going anywhere, and you don't necessarily need to ban it entirely. But diversifying your kid's digital diet is smart. These alternatives offer genuine creative outlets with better safety controls and often more educational value.

The best approach? Let your kid try a few of these. See what clicks. Maybe [Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game) becomes their main game and Roblox becomes the occasional social hangout. Maybe they discover a passion for 3D design through [Tinkercad](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/tinkercad-app). Maybe [Dreams](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/dreams-game) unlocks a future career in game development.

The goal isn't to find a perfect Roblox clone. It's to find platforms that nurture creativity without the predatory monetization and safety concerns. These seven do exactly that.

**Want more alternatives?** Check out our guides to [cozy games for kids](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/cozy-games-for-kids) or [educational games that don't feel educational](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/educational-games-that-don-t-feel-like-learning).

If you're here, you've probably already had the conversation that starts with "but all my friends play it" and ends with you Googling alternatives at 11pm.

This guide isn't anti-Roblox. Roblox is a legitimately impressive platform for the right user, and some parts of it (the official "Under 9" experience subset) are genuinely safer than the public perception. But for a 6-year-old who mainly wants to *build things*, Roblox is the wrong tool — not because it's dangerous in the hands of a supervised user, but because the risks scale with age and the building use case is served much better by dedicated creative games. Let me explain both halves of that, then walk through real alternatives.

## Why Roblox Specifically Worries Parents of 6-Year-Olds

None of this means a supervised 12-year-old can't have a great time on Roblox. It means that for a 6-year-old who mainly wants to build, the risk-to-benefit ratio is wrong.

## What 6-Year-Olds Actually Want From "Roblox"

When parents dig into why their young kid is asking for Roblox, the real answer is almost never "I want to talk to strangers and spend virtual currency." It's usually one of these:

Different alternatives serve different underlying wants. Below I've matched each option to the real desire it addresses.

## 7 Roblox Alternatives for 6-Year-Olds, Scored Honestly

| Game | Serves Which Want | Chat | Purchases | Safety | Age Fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Blocky's 3D Block Adventure** | Build stuff | None | None | ✅ Safe | 4-10 |
| **Toca Builders** | Build stuff | None | None (paid app) | ✅ Safe | 4-7 |
| **Minecraft: Creative mode, offline** | Build stuff | None (offline) | None | ✅ Safe | 7+ |
| **LEGO Creator Islands** | Build stuff | None | None | ✅ Safe | 6-10 |
| **Toca Life World** | Customize + role play | None | None (paid app) | ✅ Safe | 4-8 |
| **My PlayHome** | Role play | None | None | ✅ Safe | 3-6 |
| **Stumble Guys (under 9 with supervision)** | Play what friends play | Optional | Yes | ⚠️ Moderate | 8+ only |

A note on what's *not* on this list. Fortnite Creative is sometimes suggested as a "Roblox alternative," but it has its own chat/safety issues at scale. Among Us has chat baked in. Rec Room is VR-adjacent and aimed at older kids. I'm also deliberately excluding browser aggregators (Poki, CrazyGames, Miniplay) because the mix of quality and ad content on those sites is too inconsistent to recommend to parents of young kids.

### 📋 Get the AI Safety Checklist for Parents

10-point checklist to verify any AI tool before your child uses it. Drawn from our public review rubric.

## Matching Alternative to Actual Kid

**If your kid wants to build:** Blocky's 3D Block Adventure is the cleanest match. It's browser-based (nothing to install), has no signup or account, runs on any device, and gives a 6-year-old a structured build progression (three themed worlds, fifteen hand-designed levels) that doesn't require any reading. The core loop — pick a level, follow a ghost wireframe, build the thing, celebrate, share — is exactly the creative satisfaction most kids are trying to get from Roblox, minus the chat, purchases, and user-generated content risks.

**If your kid wants role play and customization:** Toca Life World is the gold standard. It's a paid app, but the content is extensive and there's zero social layer. My PlayHome is a simpler option for younger kids who just want to move characters around a house.

# **Your kids love video games. Which are the safest ones to play?**

![Sam Liberty](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*41-c96FhtKnOsntes5_iZQ.jpeg)

A colleague of mine has kids in grade school and high school. She’s careful about digital wellness, sets screen time limits, does all the responsible parent things. We were having coffee a few weeks ago when she asked me point blank: “What games are actually safe for my kids to play?”

She’d been researching, reading parenting blogs, trying to make sense of it all. But every time she thought she had a handle on things, her kids would come home talking about a new game all their friends were playing. Roblox, Fortnite, something on their tablets. Were these okay? Should she say yes? Were there better options?

As someone who designs games for a living, I knew the answer was more complicated than she hoped. Because here’s what most parents don’t know: the video game industry has split into two camps. One designs games as entertainment. The other designs games as psychological manipulation engines built to extract money from your kids.

The frustrating part? Both look identical to parents who aren’t familiar with the space. Both are colorful, both claim to be fun, both are popular with kids.

So I created a flag system to help her evaluate any game her kids asked about. And because I’m guessing you’re in a similar position, I’m sharing it here.

## **The Safety Flag System**

Think of this like beach flags. Green means swim freely. Yellow means caution. Red means serious risks. Double red means stay out of the water.

### **✅ Green Flag Games**

### ⚠️ **Yellow Flag Games**

### 🚩 **Red Flag Games**

### 🚩🚩 **Double Red Flag Games**

Now let’s look at the games your kids are actually asking about.

## 🚩🚩 **Roblox**

I’m starting here because this is probably the game you’re most worried about. And you should be.

Roblox hits multiple double red criteria. Around 40% of users are under 13, and on the surface it looks innocent: a creative platform where kids build and play games, kind of like Minecraft.

![]()

But the safety record is alarming. The platform faces at least 35 lawsuits alleging that users meet and abuse children on the gaming platform or that it helps facilitate child sexual exploitation and grooming. ([ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/GMA/Family/roblox-announces-new-safety-measure-amid-spate-lawsuits/story?id=127626071)) At least 30 people have been arrested since 2018 in the United States for abducting or sexually abusing children they had groomed on the platform. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_safety_on_Roblox))

The chat moderation has been particularly problematic. Users have been documented evading Roblox content and chat moderation to perform sexual content by taking activity offsite to other social media platforms, especially Discord, with applications showing that the large majority of users in these communities were under 15. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_safety_on_Roblox))

Roblox is finally implementing stronger measures. Starting in December 2024 in select markets and globally in January 2026, Roblox requires facial age verification or government ID to access chat features. ([Roblox](https://corp.roblox.com/newsroom/2025/11/roblox-requires-age-checks-limits-minor-and-adult-chat)) For children under 9, chat features are automatically turned off by default unless parents provide consent. ([ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/GMA/Family/roblox-announces-new-safety-measure-amid-spate-lawsuits/story?id=127626071))

These are improvements. But they’re reactive fixes after years of documented problems, and they don’t address the user-generated content issues or the monetization model that encourages constant spending.

But even if the moderation in the game were perfect (it isn’t), the fundamental problem with Roblox is the exploitative business model. Yes, it’s “free” to play, but each game within Roblox sets its own costs, paid not in dollars and cents but in Robux, a digital currency that obscures the actual cost of purchases. On top of that, most games require users to convert Robux into the game’s own currency, adding yet another layer of obfuscation.

If I bought 10,000,000 gems for 1,350 Robux, how much is a gem worth in dollars? Nobody knows. And that’s the point.

**If your child already plays Roblox:** Disable chat entirely for kids under 13. Use maximum parental controls. Monitor which games they’re playing within Roblox (yes, games within the game). Have regular safety conversations about never sharing personal information or moving conversations to other platforms.

**My honest take:** The risk-to-benefit ratio doesn’t make sense when safer alternatives exist. This is the one game where I think parents should feel comfortable saying no, even if “all their friends play it.”

## **✅ Minecraft**

Here’s some good news: the game that’s almost as popular as Roblox is actually one of the safest options available.

Minecraft is a sandbox game where players mine resources, craft tools, and construct structures, offering endless creativity and serving as a platform where children can build virtually anything they imagine. ([ESRB](https://www.esrb.org/blog/what-parents-need-to-know-about-minecraft/)) As kids build and explore in Minecraft, they’re immersed in creative thinking, geometry, geology, and engineering, gaining experience designing and making something from start to finish. ([BrightCanary](https://www.brightcanary.io/minecraft-parental-controls/))

Teachers around the world use Minecraft in classrooms. There’s even a dedicated Education Edition designed specifically for learning.

![]()

What makes Minecraft particularly safe is how Microsoft designed the default settings. Microsoft designed Minecraft with child safety in mind, with default settings for young children automatically disabling chat and multiplayer features. ([Familyitguy](https://www.familyitguy.com/minecraft-safety-guide.html)) Parents can control multiplayer access, chat features, and friend lists through Microsoft account settings, giving substantial control over their child’s gameplay experience. ([Minecraft](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/parental-controls))

You buy it once and that’s it. No constant monetization pressure, no aggressive FOMO tactics, no strangers in chat unless you specifically enable that.

**The one catch:** Kids can become obsessed and play for hours. The open-ended, creative nature makes it genuinely engaging (in the way Legos are engaging). But this is a time management issue, not a safety issue. Set clear boundaries about screen time and Minecraft becomes one of your best options.

**My recommendation:** Green light for ages 6 and up. For younger kids (under 10), keep them in single-player mode or set up a private realm where they only play with real-life friends. For older kids, you can gradually expand multiplayer privileges as they mature.

## ⚠️ **Fortnite**

Fortnite might surprise you. It’s probably safer than you think, but it still requires parental involvement.

Here’s what’s actually good about Fortnite: All microtransactions in Fortnite are purely cosmetic, with skins, emotes, and battle passes providing no competitive advantage. ([TekRevol](https://www.tekrevol.com/blogs/fortnite-revenue-usage-statistics/)) Your child won’t lose matches because they didn’t spend money. They won’t be at a disadvantage against kids whose parents buy them stuff. The game is genuinely free to play in full.

![]()

This is actually responsible design. Many game designers (including me) consider cosmetic-only monetization to be one of the more ethical approaches to free-to-play games.

The problem is how Fortnite sells those cosmetics. Seasonal refreshes with frequent updates and limited-time modes drive fear of missing out and purchases, with the average player spending $102 annually on cosmetics. ([TekRevol](https://www.tekrevol.com/blogs/fortnite-revenue-usage-statistics/)) Parents have sued Epic Games over limited-time sales creating a false sense of FOMO for younger players. ([PC Gamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/games/battle-royale/parents-are-suing-epic-over-fortnite-item-shop-fomo-timers-they-say-are-inaccurate-and-manipulative/))

Your kid will see a Spider-Man skin available for “24 hours only” and feel like they’re missing out if they don’t get it. They’ll see their friends with the current season’s battle pass skins and feel left behind. This is intentional design meant to create urgency and anxiety.

Fortnite also has voice chat in squad modes, which pushes it toward red flag territory. However, you can disable voice chat in the settings.

**My recommendation:** Ages 12 and up only, with firm boundaries. Set a strict spending limit (I’d suggest zero, or maybe $10/month maximum). Disable voice chat unless they’re playing with real-life friends they know from school.

Most importantly, use Fortnite as a teaching opportunity. Talk about why the game creates limited-time offers. Help your child recognize the manipulation. Ask questions like “Why do you think they only make this available for one day?” Kids are smart; once they understand they’re being manipulated, they often become more resistant to it.

For younger kids (under 12) who can’t yet critically analyze marketing tactics, I’d skip Fortnite entirely. They’re not ready for that level of psychological sophistication.

## 🚩 **/** 🚩🚩 **Free-To-Play Mobile and Tablet Games**

Now we get to the worst category: the casual games your kids download on their tablets and phones.

These are the games that show up in ads. The ones with bright colors and cute characters. The ones that look innocent but are actually designed with one primary goal: maximize revenue per user.

I can’t list every problematic game (there are thousands), but I can give you the warning signs:

![]()

### **Red flags:**

### **Double red flags:**

If a game has three or more red flags, delete it. If it has any double red flags, delete it immediately.

Let me give you a real example. My son accidentally subscribed to a “premium” coloring app that cost **$11 *per week***. He thought he was just trying out a new feature. The app was designed specifically to confuse kids about what they were signing up for. This is what we call a “dark pattern” in design: an interface deliberately created to lead users into choices they wouldn’t make if they understood what was happening.

These games use the same psychological techniques as casinos. Variable reward schedules. Artificial scarcity. Social pressure. Loss aversion. Except they’re targeting children who don’t have fully developed impulse control or the ability to recognize manipulation.

**My general rule:** If it’s free-to-play on mobile or tablet and popular with kids, assume it’s exploitative until proven otherwise. The exceptions are rare enough that this heuristic will serve you well.

## **✅ Nintendo Switch and Console Games**

Let me end with the best news: there’s an entire category of games designed with your child’s wellbeing in mind rather than your wallet.

Games like Super Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Mario Kart, and Kirby on the Nintendo Switch represent what I consider the gold standard of kids’ gaming. Nintendo has built robust parental controls into the Switch through a dedicated mobile app, allowing parents to monitor playtime, set daily limits, and restrict online features. ([Nintendo](https://www.nintendo.com/en-gb/News/2023/November/Nintendo-Switch-parental-controls-three-safety-tips-for-parents-2478405.html))

![]()

These games check every green flag box. You pay once (typically $40 to $60) and get the complete experience. No surprise charges. No psychological manipulation. No chat with strangers (most are local multiplayer only or have very limited online features). No energy systems or loot boxes or artificial scarcity.

When my son plays Mario Kart, he’s learning timing, spatial awareness, problem-solving, and how to handle both winning and losing gracefully. When he plays a typical free-to-play mobile game, he’s learning to navigate dark patterns designed by teams of behavioral psychologists.

The same goes for other console games on PlayStation and Xbox, though you’ll need to be more selective there since those platforms have a wider range of mature content. Stick to games rated E (Everyone) or E10+ (Everyone 10 and older) for younger kids.

**The catch:** The upfront cost. A Nintendo Switch costs around $300, and games are $40 to $60 each. The Switch 2 is even more expensive. For many families, this is a significant investment.

But here’s how I think about it: compare that $300 plus a few games to the “free” mobile games where kids can rack up hundreds of dollars in a few months of microtransactions. Or to Roblox where you’re paying in both money and risk. The Switch is actually the more economical option over time, plus it becomes a family activity rather than isolated screen time.

If the cost is prohibitive, consider buying used, looking for refurbished models, or even sharing a console among siblings or with another family.

## **What To Actually Do**

Okay, you’ve got the flag system and you know how the popular games stack up. Now what?

**When your child asks about a new game**, take five minutes to investigate:

**Set up systems, not rules.** Instead of arguing about each individual game, create a framework:

For younger kids (under 8): Primarily offline games or heavily supervised play. Minecraft in single-player mode. Nintendo games. No chat with anyone they don’t know in real life.

For older kids (8 to 12): Expand to carefully monitored multiplayer. Private Minecraft realms with friends. Maybe Fortnite with strict spending limits and disabled voice chat. Regular conversations about manipulation tactics.

For teens (13+): More freedom but maintained awareness. They’re old enough to learn about manipulative design. Use games as teaching opportunities: “Why do you think they designed it this way? What are they trying to make you feel?”

**Play with your kids.** Not just watching over their shoulder, but actually playing. You’ll understand what they’re experiencing, you’ll spot problems faster, and honestly, many of these games are more fun than you’d expect. Some of my best conversations with my kids have happened while building something together in Minecraft or competing in Mario Kart.

![]()

## **The Big Picture**

My colleague left that coffee conversation with a plan. She felt equipped to make decisions instead of just reacting to whatever her kids brought home next.

The video game industry isn’t going to fix this on its own (there’s too much money at stake), and regulatory efforts are slow. That leaves us parents to be the gatekeepers. It’s not being overprotective to say no to Roblox. It’s not being mean to set spending limits on Fortnite. It’s not being out of touch to delete exploitative mobile games.

You’re being exactly what your kids need, even if they don’t realize it yet.

So the next time your child asks for that game all their friends have, you’ll know exactly how to evaluate it. And more importantly, you’ll know you’re making an informed choice rather than just hoping for the best.

Your kids will thank you later. Even if right now they’re just annoyed you won’t let them download whatever showed up in a YouTube ad.
